newsitem.title: BELGIUM: More beef, BSE battles seen during Dutch presidency.
newsitem.headline: More beef, BSE battles seen during Dutch presidency.

text.p: Further beef battles are looming during the first half of 1997 as member states fight over long- term reforms to deal with the mad cow crisis and Britain strives to ease a worldwide beef ban, Dutch and EU officials said.

They said Dutch Farm Minister Jozias Van Aartsen will also highlight the 1997/98 farm price package and the need to continue farm reforms started in 1992 when he presents the Dutch presidency's programme to EU farm ministers on January 20.

"Beef reforms and BSE are likely to dominate the presidency agenda," a Dutch official said, referring to Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), the fatal cattle brain disease that has ravaged mainly British herds.
The Netherlands, an important dairy producer, also intends to start serious discussion on reform of the EU's milk quota scheme, though this would not be directly linked to beef reforms.
- MAD COW CRISIS:

1) BSE: British Farm Minister Douglas Hogg told EU farm ministers last month he would present proposals early in 1997, probably February, to exempt certified herds from the worldwide ban imposed by the EU last March after London disclosed that BSE could be transmitted to humans in the form of Creutzfeldt Jacob Disease.
Northern Irish herds certified to be free of BSE could be the first to be exempted, Dutch farm ministry spokesman Henri Kruithof told reporters in The Hague last week.
Northern Irish herds are generally fed on grass -- unlike English herds which were given contaminated meat and bone meal -- and their movements are tracked by a computerised system.
Kruithof cautioned against any early easing of the ban, saying it will take at least two years to extend the tracking system to the whole of Britain.
The British proposals would have to be agreed by the Commission, EU veterinary committees and by member states.
Several countries, notably Germany, are expected to resist any early easing of the ban while uncertainties exist about the cause and eradication of the disease.
Exemption of certified herds would be the first step towards lifting the worldwide ban on British beef exports under an agreement reached at the June European Council in Florence.
It followed Britain's announcement last month that it will cull an extra 100,000 cattle most at risk to BSE. The cull is the fifth and final pre-condition set under the Florence accord.
But the cull could be raised, depending on scientific advice due in March on data that BSE can be passed from cows to calves.

2) BEEF REFORMS: The Commission is due to present proposals by the end of April for long-term measures to cut production to bring it into line with a fall in demand due to the public health scare over mad cow disease.
When farm ministers agreed a package of short term measures last October, they asked the Commission to draft further proposals within six months so that a decision could be taken by the end of 1997.

Longer-term measures could include a reduction in national quotas of male cattle receiving EU subsidies, incentives for less intensive grass-fed herds and a restructuring of livestock production. A reinforced beef promotion campaign and a reduction in carcasse weight limits for cattle sold into intervention could also form part of the package.
On January 20, farm ministers are due to discuss again proposals to introduce cattle passport and beef labelling schemes intended to help restore consumer confidence.
- PRICE PACKAGE:
Commission price proposals for 1997/98 (July/June), expected early February, are again likely to be fairly modest, Commission officials said.

Farm support prices and compensation payments look set to remain unchanged although Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler may again try to cut monthly increases in grain storage payments. A fresh bid may be made to cut monthly sugar storage refunds.
"The package is likely to be very small...mainly a rollover of existing measures," a Commission official said.
The aim is to consolidate the 1992 reform of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and take account of subsidy-cutting and market-opening measures under the world farm trade accord.
But ministers are again expected to resort to traditional tactics of trying to add "sweeteners" for their farmers and negotiations could drag on into June.
However the margin for manoeuvre is greatly reduced by the 1.6-billion-Ecu cost of the mad cow crisis.
The 1997 farm budget has been capped at 40.8 billion Ecus, unchanged from last year, after finance ministers rejected a proposed 1.0-billion-Ecu increase.
- FARM REFORMS:
1) OLIVE OIL: The Commission is expected to present proposals on January 23 to reform the olive oil marketing regime, simplifying subsidies and curbing costly fraud.
Southern European farmers are concerned that the reforms will lead to a reduction in both olive oil quality and income.
The reform will be the latest in a series started in 1992 with oilseeds and cereals, aimed at removing surplus production and cutting costs.
2) TOBACCO: Farm ministers are due to start discussing on January 20 a Commission report urging reforms to improve tobacco quality and incentives for farmers to stop growing tobacco.
The report was adopted on December 18 despite strong criticism that continuation of tobacco subsidies hindered efforts to curb smoking-related deaths.
Fischler successfully argued that ending the subsidies would put 300,000 people out of work in Greece and Italy with little prospect of finding other work.

- DAIRY REFORM: Although the current milk quota system only expires at the end of March 2000, the Dutch are keen to press ahead with discussion of reforms to prepare for the next round of world farm trade negotiations starting in 1999 and the EU's enlargement eastwards.
The Commission is due to present a discussion paper, setting out options, in time for a preliminary discussion at an informal meeting of farm ministers in Domburg, Zeeland, from May 25-27.

An independent report advocating the abolition of the milk quota system and a sharp cut in prices to prevent an explosion in production was criticised by EU member state officials in Killarney, Ireland, in September.

- ANIMAL WELFARE: The Dutch will try to get agreement on Commission proposals of December 13 fixing minimum standards for farm animal resting points during long distance journeys. The proposals concern Directive 91/628 and set norms for feeding, watering, loading and unloading from vehicles.
Changes were also proposed for route plans so as to ensure enforcement of resting point rules.
- MEAT HORMONES:
A World Trade Organisation disputes panel is due to meet in Geneva on October 10 to hear Washington's complaint against the EU's ban on imports of beef treated with growth hormones.

The United States, along with Australia, New Zealand and Canada, say that the meat is safe and the ban is not scientifically justified. But Fischler has said that consumer concerns must be safeguarded.
The WTO panel is not expected to reach a preliminary conclusion on the U.S. and other complaints until at least April 1997.

- BANANAS: A WTO disputes panel is due to rule in February on a complaint from the United States that EU banana import quotas favour Caribbean producers and breach free trade rules. The Commission is expected to appeal against any adverse ruling.

Meanwhile a Commission proposal (COM(95)115) to increase the import quota for "dollar" bananas by 353,000 tonnes to 2.53 million tonnes to cater for new members Austria, Sweden and Finland remains blocked. So is a proposal (COM(95)114) to exclude small fig bananas from the banana regime (EEC/404/93).
Germany, backed by the new members, opposes the proposals unless the EU increases imports of cheaper "dollar" bananas from Latin America.

- CEREAL/OILSEED PENALTIES: Another attempt may be made at the January Farm Council to unblock Commission proposals (COM(96)175) presented last June 12 to make penalties for overplanting more flexible. In December, demands from six member states for even greater flexibility were rejected by the Commission because they would weaken 1992 reforms to reduce surpluses.

- DURUM WHEAT: A proposal presented on July 30, 1996 (COM(96)361) to change the durum wheat aid scheme remains blocked. The Commission proposed a maximum guaranteed area for each member state to be shared between traditional producers. It also proposed the compulsory use of certified seed and anti- fraud measures to ensure that output matched the planted area.
When last discussed in November, Fischler told farm ministers that their demands for an extra 650,000 hectares to be included in the aid scheme would cost 200 million Ecus and were unacceptable.

- WINE REFORM: Little progress is expected on proposals to remove wine surpluses and improve quality (COM(94)117). They have been held up by strong opposition from southern producer countries which said quota cuts were too great and compensation too low. Fischler said in response to Italy's arguement that the wine surplus had disappeared that the Commission would study whether the improved market situation was due to structural or cyclical factors, notably poor weather.

- VETERINARY ISSUES: An April 1 deadline has been set for reaching veterinary equivalency agreements with the United States, Australia, various Latin American and other trading partners. So far agreement on mutual recognition of veterinary standards and inspection rules has only been reached with New Zealand.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration's proposal earlier this month to ban feed containing reprocessed spinal cord and other suspect animal tissue should, if adopted, help resolve problems over U.S. petfood exports, EU officials said.

Veterinary and Phytosanitary Inspection Agency: In a statement at the Farm Council on November 21, the Commission strongly complained about the lack of resources for the new agency to be located in Grange, County Meath, Ireland. It said that current staffing of 20 permanent and 11 temporary officials was insufficient. In addition it was very difficult to persuade permanent officials to move to Ireland from Brussels.
Member states have been at odds over the funding and status of the new agency.

- FLAX AND HEMP REFORM: Ministers are due to start discussing on January 20 a Commission proposal to introduce a maximum guaranteeed area for fibre flax in 1997/98 (July/June). The proposal (COM(96)629) also seeks to cut aid for farmers using cheaper new production methods. Controls would be introduced to ensure that aid is only given for flax and hemp where there is a market outlet.
- EASTERN EUROPE: EU farm ministers and their eastern European counterparts are due to discuss veterinary and phytosanitary standards and inspection rules during the March 17/18 Farm Council.
The meeting is part of a series to prepare for the EU membership of up to 10 former communist countries from central and eastern Europe.

- FARM REFORM: The Commission may present a discussion paper in March or April on further reform of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). It would follow up an agricultural strategy paper of November 1995 looking at options to prepare for the EU's expansion eastwards (see Commission statement IP/95/1314).

- RURAL DEVELOPMENT: The Commission may also present a discussion paper in March on an integrated rural development policy. It would follow-up the November Cork Declaration, which has stirred growing opposition from member states, notably Germany, and from farmers.
They are concerned about a possible draining of funds from farmers towards tourism and other rural economic activities and an undermining of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).

- REGIONAL FOOD: A fresh attempt will be made during the Dutch presidency to agree on the transitional period for member states to adapt to new rules to protect feta cheese and other regional food items.
The original regulation 2081/92 set up a five-year transitional period expiring on July 24, 1997.
The Commission has proposed that the new rules should apply after a further five-year period expiring on July 24, 2002.
Some member states, such as Denmark, want an even longer delay.
- MOUNTAIN AGRICULTURE: Austria, Italy and France will continue to press for a follow-up to memorandums requesting changes in aid schemes for mountain farmers.
